prize_parts.citation: for integrating formal theory and empirical analysis to show how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my preferred single-achievement prize. Persson, Tabellini and Besley turned government from a benevolent planner into an endogenous actor whose behaviour depends on electoral rules, constitutional design, accountability and state capacity. They did this with formal models matched to testable predictions, for example on electoral systems, forms of government and the composition of spending. The attribution is the cleanest among the leading candidates. Persson and Tabellini form the constitutional and electoral-rules programme, and Besley supplies the complementary state-capacity and political-agency strand. The contributions are 25 to 30 years old and have been extended and tested in many datasets. It is distinct from the 2024 institutions prize. That prize answered whether inclusive institutions cause long-run prosperity, using colonial history. This work asks how specific institutional rules inside a given polity change policy choices and fiscal outcomes. The two are complementary in the way I described in the 2024 presentation speech: the 2024 question was causal, and this one concerns mechanisms and commitment.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. The theory is general and elegant, but much of the cross-country evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects rests on observational variation and contested identification. As someone who builds and uses comparative regime data, I know how sensitive such findings are to classification and measurement choices. A second concern is that the Committee may judge the 2024 prize to have already covered the institutions theme, so a neighbouring award could look redundant. A third is that a three-name prize forces a choice about how to frame the contribution (constitutions and electoral rules, or state capacity), and that choice affects whether Besley is included.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first on breadth of policy influence and ranks B006 second. He calls B006 mature, with three decades of confirmation across many empirical settings, and arguably overdue. He also discloses an institutional proximity to Persson.
responses.response: I agree that maturity is not an obstacle for B006. I would not rest the case on 'overdue', since time elapsed is not evidence of merit. I also do not follow him in putting B001 first. The choice of Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is defensible, but he and several others concede that Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have comparable claims. That leaves the B001 attribution less clean than B006, where the three credited names are the recognisable core of one programme. I note his disclosure and keep it separate from the scientific assessment.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B002 first because Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of collateral-constraint amplification. He ranks B006 fourth and proposes only Persson and Tabellini, saying that excluding Besley is a difficult judgement.
responses.response: I share his view of B002. It is my second choice because the two-author attribution is unusually clean and the mechanism is foundational. I disagree on dropping Besley from B006. His work on state capacity and political agency is an independent strand with its own body of evidence, and it is the part most relevant to long-run state-building questions. Excluding him would shrink the discovery to constitutions and electoral rules. That is why I keep three names. I accept that a two-person prize would be a legitimate fallback if the Committee prefers a narrower framing.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B006 second but flags that the 2024 institutions prize may reduce appetite for another political-economy award so soon, and that causal identification in the constitutional-effects work is open to challenge.
responses.response: Both concerns are fair and are the reservations I weight most heavily. On the first, I would not treat topic adjacency as a bar. What matters is whether the discovery is distinct. The 2024 prize rests on causal evidence about colonial-era institutions and long-run income. This work analyses how rules within a polity shape policy choices, and it uses different theory and methods. On the second, I accept that the theory outruns the identification. But the programme's contribution is the framework and the testable predictions, and later design-based work has refined the evidence rather than overturned it.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B021 first, treating Melitz (2003) as central and Helpman as completing the core. He ranks B006 fifth and discloses Persson's links to the committee and IIES as a possible conflict.
responses.response: I accept his argument that B021 is a mature, high-impact candidate with a clear core. I rank it fourth, after B006, B002 and B001, because the credit boundary with the empirical firm-level pioneers (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum), who are off the ballot, is less clean than the B006 attribution. On institutional proximity, I take his disclosure at face value and read the conflict as one to disclose, not adjudicate. I make my own disclosure below.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the 2024 institutions prize as covering this territory, or sees the within-polity rules and policy-outcomes programme as a distinct discovery.
Whether the prize is better framed around constitutions and electoral rules (Persson and Tabellini only) or also around state capacity and accountability (adding Besley).
How much weight the cross-country constitutional evidence can bear given contested identification; I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.

Whether B001 deserves to rank above B006 if the Committee can find a defensible three-person cut among Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali and Gertler; I see its attribution as unresolved, not as a weakness of the underlying science.
statement.conflict_note: No direct personal or collaborative tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley is apparent from my supplied profile. There is field proximity: I work on comparative democratisation, quality of government and state-building, which neighbours this literature, and I should not let that familiarity inflate its merit. I am at Stockholm University, where my profile lists committee colleagues in a different department (IIES), and Krusell's opening says Persson is an IIES colleague. I have not verified that. My profile lists co-authored work on corruption with 'Persson' and Rothstein (Governance) without specifying which Persson, so I make no claim that this is Torsten Persson. I also note that the 2024 presentation speech I gave does not establish a private preference.
